title: Beyond Blood Cultures and Echocardiography: Emerging Diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis.
abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.

title: Generative artificial intelligence in medical oncology: A clinically focused narrative review of large language, vision-language, and agentic artificial intelligence systems.
abstract: Rapid advances in cancer genetics and genomics, pathophysiology, diagnostics, and therapeutics have substantially increased the complexity of clinical oncology. Integrating large and diverse data streams into timely, patient-specific decisions provides a compelling rationale for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into cancer care. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) encompasses several classes of models capable of generating new content. This clinically focused review concentrates on GenAI applications based primarily on large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), as well as emerging agentic systems that use these models to perform coordinated, multistep tasks. LLMs demonstrate substantial medical knowledge, strong performance on oncology-related assessments, and emerging capabilities in clinical reasoning. Guideline- and retrieval-augmented systems can improve concordance with expert recommendations and interpretation of complex treatment algorithms. LLMs and VLMs have been applied to documentation, patient communication, information extraction and summarization, clinical decision support, and multimodal data synthesis. However, performance varies substantially across tasks and clinical domains, with important limitations including incomplete or outdated information, training-data bias, automation bias, and confabulation. Agentic AI represents an emerging extension of these technologies in which LLMs or VLMs are incorporated into systems capable of multistep planning, external information retrieval, specialized tool use, and iterative evaluation and refinement. Early oncology applications include evidence synthesis, multimodal clinical decision support, radiology, pathology, surgery, and individualized treatment planning. With rigorous validation, transparent implementation, continual updating, and appropriate expert oversight, GenAI may augment oncologists' judgment, improve patient understanding and experience, streamline cancer care delivery, and advance personalized oncology.

title: Multi-omics uncover interactions in the vaginal microbiome and a type II secretion/Tad pilus system in Gardnerella species
abstract: Background: The vaginal microbiome is a key determinant of women's health, with Lactobacillus-dominant communities protecting against bacterial vaginosis (BV) and related adverse outcomes. Dysbiosis involves a decline in lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes, with Gardnerella species central to initiating polymicrobial aggregates. However, the genetic determinants of community assembly, biofilm formation, and interspecies interactions remain poorly understood. This study investigated the genomic and functional basis of these traits using an integrated multi-omics approach. Results: Long-read whole-genome sequencing of clinical Gardnerella isolates yielded closed genomes and revealed a pangenomic split correlating with high- versus low-biofilm phenotypes, linked to clade-specific genomic islands and allelic variants. Functional gene modules within these regions distinguished G. vaginalis from G. piotii, contributing to nutrient acquisition, cell wall metabolism, and colonization. Integrated 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and proteomics of all pairwise dual-species co-cultures of five key vaginal bacteria showed that G. vaginalis and L. iners acted as dominant ecological drivers, outcompeting neighbors and triggering asymmetric proteomic remodeling. Differential expression of a gene within a putative operon encoding a conserved type II secretion/Tad pilus system, revealed by integrating the pangenome with the proteome, implicated this system in interspecies interactions. AI-based structural predictions of the complex suggested isoform-specific differences in protein folding between G. vaginalis and G. piotii. In parallel, metagenomic analysis of 93 women showed the operon was more abundant in BV samples than in healthy controls, linking it to dysbiosis. Integrated metabolomics further identified a methyl-{beta}-carboline compound elevated in Prevotella bivia-containing co-cultures that selectively inhibited G. vaginalis and P. bivia while sparing L. crispatus. Several dipeptides influenced growth and biofilm formation of vaginal microbes, and methyl-{beta}-carboline and sphingosine additionally inhibited multidrug-resistant pathogens, suggesting new strategies for managing polymicrobial infections. Conclusions: This work links Gardnerella genomic features to virulence-associated phenotypes and demonstrates how interspecies interactions shape community dynamics and antimicrobial metabolite production. The findings support a model in which biofilm capacity is genetically encoded within an accessory genome, deployed through tailored proteomic responses, and modulated by an interaction-specific metabolic landscape, providing a foundation for identifying bioactive molecules and developing diagnostics and targeted therapeutics to restore and maintain vaginal health.

title: Using iterative agentic retrieval-augmented generation to refine the risk of infection from social contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic: Development and Evaluation Study
abstract: Background: Contact tracing is crucial to limit pathogen transmission and to gather epidemiological data. However, despite machine learning optimizations, it remains time-consuming. Large language models have been used for infection risk prediction, but no existing application converses with a user to adapt its risk estimates. Objective: We aimed to develop an iterative retrieval-augmented generation conversational framework to predict coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection risk from textual social data. The conversational agent aims to gather personalized risk factors based on descriptions of social interactions. Methods: We trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict the risk of COVID-19 infection from 19,434 textual descriptions of social interactions, collected during the pandemic in the Leuven student community, in Belgium. We integrated this model into a Llama3.3-based conversational framework that iteratively gathers additional social information that may represent a risk of infection. We evaluated the framework using large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics and by comparing its risk assessment in different social contexts. Results: Based solely on social interaction data, a fine-tuned RobBERT model predicted infection risk with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.73. It performed similarly to an LSTM model and a logistic regression on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features, which both achieved a ROC AUC of 0.72. These three models slightly outperformed a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-fine-tuned Mistral NeMo model (ROC AUC = 0.69). Llama3.3 performed well in our framework: the predicted infection risk converged often, and it asked fewer redundant questions than the smaller models (Mistral 7B, Gemma3 12B). In addition, the framework showed the ability to stratify, by risk of infection, synthetic users who had different types of social interactions. Conclusions: Combining simple language models with large language models can refine individual infection risk from contact tracing data in a high-circulation context. Our conversational framework may help optimize contact tracing by highlighting social contexts with a high risk of infection.

title: Emerging advances in multimodal AI in cancer immunotherapy: from multi-scale data integration to clinical decision support.
abstract: Immunotherapy is increasingly reshaping the therapeutic landscape of clinical oncology by inducing effective tumor regression and durable responses in various types of human cancers. However, a substantial fraction of patients resist immunotherapy, or even experience relapse after an initial response. Clinically, the conventional biomarkers often exhibit limited predictive accuracy and poor transferability across tumor types. These limitations highlight the urgent need for more robust, data-driven strategies to decipher tumor-immune dynamics and guide personalized treatment. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in immuno-oncology, offering scalable solutions to decode high-dimensional and heterogeneous biomedical data. The evolution of AI can be broadly divided into six key stages: early machine learning (ML) classifiers, unsupervised representation learning, graph-based modeling of cell-cell interactions, multimodal foundation and biomedical language models, reinforcement and active learning paradigms, and AI virtual cells. At the molecular level, AI facilitates the integration of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and spatially resolved single-cell omics, supporting fine-grained reconstruction of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). At the clinical interface, the application of deep learning (DL) in liquid biopsy, digital pathology, and radiologic imaging has advanced response prediction, biomarker discovery, and early detection of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), driving personized immunotherapy. This review synthesizes recent progress in AI-guided precision immunotherapy across molecular, cellular, and phenotypic area. By outlining key methodological advances and translational opportunities, we highlight that multimodal AI frameworks can pave the way toward the more interpretable, robust, and individualized immunotherapy strategies for cancer treatment.

title: An Agentic AI Pipeline for an Evidence-Grounded Environmental Health Public Information System: Development and Evaluation
abstract: Background: Existing environmental and health information systems typically provide isolated data streams, requiring users to interpret heterogeneous information sources without personalized guidance. Residents and health providers of urban regions with complex environmental conditions, such as the Salt Lake Valley, frequently seek timely, location-specific information about weather, air quality, and their associated health impacts, but may find it difficult to integrate this information in their decision-making, precluding the effective translation of valuable environmental health information into action. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline that delivers evidence-grounded, neighborhood-scale responses to health-related environmental questions raised lay persons by dynamically orchestrating authoritative weather, neighborhood-scale environmental observations, air quality, and health-evidence resources. Methods: We developed an agentic AI pipeline using LangGraph and OpenAI large language models to interpret natural language queries, select and invoke relevant external tools, retrieve real-time environmental data and evidence-based health guidance, and synthesize responses. The pipeline integrates multiple authoritative resources, including weather forecasts, air-quality observations, geospatial services, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module built from asthma-related clinical guidance. The system incorporates fallback mechanisms to improve robustness when external services are unavailable. We evaluated the pipeline using a curated benchmark of representative user questions, assessing tool-needed recognition, correct tool selection, avoidance of irrelevant tools, parameter mapping, analytic pathway selection, and incorporation of tool outputs into the final response. Results: The developed system successfully integrated heterogeneous environmental and health information sources into a unified conversational interface that produces evidence-grounded, neighborhood-scale responses for the Salt Lake Valley. Evaluation demonstrated generally strong tool recognition, parameter mapping, and incorporation of retrieved information across diverse question types, supporting the pipeline's ability to retrieve and integrate authoritative environmental and health information consumable by lay persons and providing an important step for the T3 and T4 phases of the translational pipeline of exposure health informatics. Conclusions: By combining existing environmental health knowledge with local sensor observations and neighborhood-scale environmental measurements, and authoritative state and national weather and air quality resources, the system delivers more localized and context-aware guidance than approaches that rely on authoritative regional or state-level information. Rather than depending on the internal knowledge of a large language model, the pipeline dynamically retrieves, synthesizes, and attributes evidence from authoritative sources. The modular architecture enables seamless integration of additional environmental data streams, health knowledge sources, and geographic regions, providing a scalable foundation for future translational pipelines, completing the T3 to T4 path for environmental health.

title: Medical students and clinical teachers experiences and perceptions of using AI-based simulated patients in psychiatry clinical skills training, a qualitative analysis
abstract: Objectives: To explore medical students' and clinical teachers' experiences and perceptions of an AI-based simulated patient using a large language model (LLM-ASP) for psychiatry clinical skills training, to inform its development and integration. Design: Qualitative focus group study with reflexive thematic analysis. Setting: Kent and Medway Medical School, UK. Student groups met in person and online; teacher groups met online. Participants: Sixteen undergraduate medical students (years 3 and 4; two focus groups) and nine psychiatry clinical teachers (six residents, three consultants; three focus groups), recruited through university mailing lists and the Royal College of Psychiatrists' South Eastern Division newsletter. Interventions: Before each discussion, participants used an LLM-ASP tool built by the research team (ChatGPT Advanced Voice Mode, Streamlit, LangChain) for about 10 minutes. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis with Saldana's multi cycle coding. Results: Students and teachers each generated three themes. Students described the interface (trust, realism, reliability), educational value, and ethical, cultural and governance considerations. Teachers described pedagogical value, design and usability, and ethical, cultural and governance considerations. Both groups saw LLM-ASP as a flexible, low-pressure, self-paced supplement for early communication skills practice and for rehearsing scenarios hard to access in placements, not a replacement for actor-based simulation or patient contact. Barriers included limited emotional realism, robotic delivery and response delays. Shared ethical concerns were safeguarding, data storage and consent, accountability, demographic bias in generated patients, and over-reliance weakening critical thinking. Students also raised the impact on simulated-patient actors. Students focused on trust and usability; teachers focused on pedagogical integration and oversight. Conclusions: Participants saw LLM-ASP as a potentially useful complement to existing psychiatry teaching. Adoption depends on technical reliability, realism, representation and governance, and on keeping human interaction central to the curriculum.

title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
abstract: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested, because doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies. Given a source manuscript and a target scRNA-seq dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, and reports which findings transfer and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million RNA sequence--structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks among the leading models in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold3 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development.

title: MutQA: A Cross-Validated Q&A Dataset for Genetic Mutations
abstract: We introduce MutQA, a dataset of 330,387 citation-grounded question-answer (QA) pairs linking genetic mutations to their functional consequences as described in the biomedical literature. Each record pairs a protein-coding mutation with a natural-language question and an evidence-backed answer anchored to sentences in one of 27,442 open-access PubMed Central articles, spanning 6,620 genes and 125,593 gene-variant pairs. The dataset is constructed using CrossValQA, a framework that enforces information isolation between independent LLMs: one model generates QA pairs from an article, a second model answers the same question without access to the first model's response, and a third model judges whether each model's rationale supports the other's answer, so that retained QA pairs are reproducible from the source text rather than hallucinated. Of 401,406 audited QA pairs, 82.7% pass both directions of this cross-validation; those with a recoverable reference protein sequence form the released benchmark. In a 999-pair stratified audit, two expert annotators agree exactly on 86.4% of cross-validated QA pairs (95% CI 83.7-89.0; n = 638), a tier in which about 90% of ratings are "correct". Individual LLM judges agree with individual annotators at a comparable 87.0% on this tier but far less on QA pairs that fail cross-validation. Fine-tuning MutaPLM on MutQA nearly doubles its mean LLM-judge score for question-conditioned mutation-effect answering (1.45 to 2.82 on a 0-5 scale) and improves mutation-recovery accuracy from effect descriptions from 19.4% to 32.1%. Providing variant-matched MutQA retrieval context, without fine-tuning, improves strict answer accuracy across four LLM families by 20.0-28.6 percentage points, demonstrating the framework's ability to improve the reliability of LLM answers. We also apply CrossValQA to proteomics, providing a proof of concept for its use beyond mutation-specific QA. We release the dataset, construction framework, and evaluation code.

title: Efficient biological design via genomic in-context learning
abstract: In-context learning (ICL), the ability to perform new tasks from a few examples supplied in a prompt, is a defining emergent capability of large language models. Here, we show that ICL emerges in the genome language model Evo 2 and enables biological design. With as few as four examples in the prompt and no additional training, Evo 2 generates realistic metal-binding proteins, de novo antibodies, protein-RNA systems, and entire bacteriophage genomes. For {Phi}X174-like bacteriophage design, ICL surpasses previously fine-tuned models on computational measures of design quality and diversity. Beyond {Phi}X174, conditioning the model with different phage prompts enables us to efficiently design MS2 and M13 genomes in silico without fine-tuning. Iteratively updating the prompt with newly generated phage genomes, which we refer to as genomic chain-of-thought, further improves the diversity of designs while maintaining quality metrics. Paired with an inference engine that accelerates generation up to 35-fold and extends practicable context to a megabase, these results establish ICL as a versatile and efficient paradigm for biological sequence design.

title: Lineage-mixed neurodevelopmental programs in pediatric sarcomas nominate tumor-selective surface antigen pairs.
abstract: Pediatric solid tumors have low mutational burden, frequent oncogenic gene fusions, and developmental origins in arrested progenitor cells. Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) could represent an ideal tool to assess whether these convergent biological features yield shared therapeutic vulnerabilities. However, while existing tools can extract gene expression programs for pan-tumor single-cell data, interpreting them requires domain expertise across many disciplines and diseases. Here, we analyzed a pan-pediatric scRNA-seq atlas of 266 patient- and xenograft-derived samples across 22 pediatric solid tumor types. To address the bottleneck between gene program identification and interpretation, we developed an AI agent framework built on off-the-shelf large language models (e.g., Gemini 2.5) to interpret gene expression programs at the level of human experts, but at much greater scale and speed. Our agent identified ectopic expression of neuronal marker genes as a unique feature of several fusion-driven sarcomas. This gene expression pattern resulted in tumor-specific co-expression of mixed mesenchymal/neuronal surface markers, providing a plausible therapeutic window to target these tumor types using emerging AND-gated therapeutic strategies, such as bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and bispecific CAR-T cells. As proof of principle, we nominated and validated STEAP1/NPTXR as a Ewing sarcoma candidate cell surface target pair. Together, this work delivers a pan-pediatric solid tumor scRNA-seq atlas, establishes a generalizable and accessible AI-based framework that complements existing single-cell methods by automating interpretation of pan-disease single-cell atlases, and nominates new bispecific ADC/CAR-T targets for catastrophic pediatric cancers.

title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

title: A Deep Learning Model for Prediction of Unknown Gene Functionality: Gene Bio-BERT.
abstract: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was a large international research effort that timelined between 1990 and 2003, marking the successful mapping of the entire human genome. Despite the promising performance of deep learning models, especially LLMs like Bio-BERT and ProtBERT on well-annotated datasets. Bio-BERT is a pre-trained language model designed for biomedical corpora, it is not able to independently predict gene functionality. A pre-trained model called ProtBERT uses protein sequences to learn features. It is unable to predict gene functionality directly, without more training data. In order to overcome these challenges, a Gene Bio-BERT based framework is proposed for automated gene function prediction utilizing deep learning methods in biomedical data analysis. This Gene Bio-BERT Framework is divided into 3 modules such as Data collection and Preprocessing, Gene Bio-BERT model training, Feature aggregation layer and prediction of functionality. The initial module focuses on data collection and preprocessing. Data is collected using entrez API from NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information) to retrieve human gene data. Preprocessing techniques like Tokenization and feature extraction are then used to handle the data. In the second module, a Gene Bio-BERT transformer encoder with an attention-based feature fusion layer and optimized hyperparameters is used to train the model and learn contextual embeddings. The third module generates results by using aggregated transformer representations to produce functional predictions for unknown genes. In predicting gene function, the proposed Gene Bio-BERT model attains an exceptional accuracy of 94.5% and F1 score of 0.87. Additionally, the model's predictive accuracy remains similar when tested on an unannotated gene which gives similarity score 0.84.

title: Transforming one health antimicrobial resistance surveillance in resource-limited countries (RLCs): From point-of-care diagnostics to AI-driven decision support.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major and escalating global problem, particularly for resource-limited countries (RLCs) with limited capacity to diagnose diseases, inadequate surveillance systems, insufficient antimicrobial stewardship, and poor health facilities. Conventional AMR surveillance relies primarily on post hoc laboratory reporting and is not able to provide real-time data to aid in making effective clinical and public health decisions. AMR surveillance is being revolutionized with the introduction of point-of-care (PoC) diagnostics, digital health technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) that offer rapid pathogen identification, real-time data collection, and predictive analysis. This review highlights the evolution of the AMR surveillance system from conventional lab-based techniques to using AI and data to inform decision-making for RLCs. Evidence is being collected on new PoC diagnostic platforms, biosensors, genomic surveillance, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and machine learning (ML) algorithms developed from clinical, microbiological, genomic, and epidemiological data to help improve resistance detection, antimicrobial prescribing, antimicrobial stewardship, and outbreak prediction. We also explore the challenges of implementation, such as lack of digital infrastructure, data interoperability, workforce capacity, algorithmic bias, ethical and regulatory considerations, and sustainable funding in AMR surveillance. The potential of new innovations like Mobile health (mHealth), Internet of Things (IoT), Federated Learning (FL), and AI is highlighted as necessary tools to help ensure greater scale, transparency, and equitable deployment. Lastly, we suggest an integrated approach, which brings together AMR PoC diagnostics, clinical decision support using AI, and One Health surveillance to improve the monitoring and response to AMR. Therefore, this review provides a pathway to implementing resilient, intelligent, and equitable AMR surveillance systems and illustrates how technological innovation can be linked to AMR system implementation for better patient outcomes and implementation of evidence-based public health policies in RLCs.

title: Ground-truth evaluation of sparse autoencoder features on spatial, single-cell and language-model embeddings
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used to extract interpretable features from the embeddings of biological foundation models. Because SAEs trained with different random seeds learn different features, reproducibility across seeds has become a common test of whether these features can be trusted. We asked whether reproducible features are also meaningful, using embeddings whose concepts are known: five spatial transcriptomics embeddings of two colorectal cancer sections and Geneformer embeddings of single-cell RNA profiles, with cell lineages as concepts; synthetic data with planted cell states; and the residual stream of a small language model, with token classes as concepts. Varimax rotations of the same embeddings were almost perfectly reproducible, yet rotation features (PCA, varimax and ICA) covered at most three of seven lineages and three of eight token classes. Single SAE fits showed the opposite profile: they covered most concepts with purer gene programs but reproduced only 27-46% of their features. A consensus over five SAE fits combined the two strengths. It was reproducible (78-98% across sources) and as pure as single fits: 11-40% of its features carried marker genes of another lineage, against 44-70% for varimax. Against the strongest baseline, varimax sparsified to the SAE's sparsity, the consensus covered as many concepts on PCA and Geneformer embeddings and more on learned spatial and text embeddings. The consensus also had costs. It covered fewer lineages than single fits and, like all SAEs, missed weak planted states that rotations recovered; neither a longer single fit nor a second SAE trained on the consensus residual recovered what it discarded. Reproducibility alone therefore ranks features poorly: SAE features should be reported with the number of known concepts they cover and the purity of their gene programs, against a rotation of the same embedding sparsified to the SAE's sparsity.

title: Multi-resolution humanness scoring of antibodies via a region-isolated language model
abstract: Antibodies recognized as foreign can elicit anti-drug antibodies that compromise efficacy and safety, making humanness scoring, estimating how human-like a sequence appears, an early, repeated step in antibody development. Widely used scores reduce a variable domain to a single framework-dominated number, leaving the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) grafted during humanization, diversified by generative models weakly supervised and rarely audited. Here we introduce IgScope, a 23-million-parameter antibody language model trained from scratch that scores humanness at chain, IMGT-region, and residue resolution; a region-isolated attention module confines attention to within-region pairs, and chimeric-sequence training supplies region-level supervision. On 2.38 million held-out chains, masking all framework tokens leaves CDR accuracy unchanged, and back-mutated murine residues in human frameworks are detected at 93.4% accuracy. At chain level, IgScope matches the strongest published correlation with clinical anti-drug-antibody incidence (r = 0.567, n = 217) and outperforms a same-protocol recomputation. Region-level scoring exposes what chain-level scoring conceals: antibodies designed de novo by four generative models pass whole-chain humanness (0.966-0.988), while their CDRs score far below natural (P < 1e-30) in every chain class. Quality control turns the same resolution to the mirror-image question: in humanized-mouse platforms, whose domains are human by design, IgScope scores the domain as human and, in HUGO-Nano chimeric VHHs, isolates only the FR2 signal of four camelid hallmark residues deliberately retained to stabilize the VHH. IgScope gives antibody humanization a verified foundation and generative design an audit.

title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents. The project repository is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauProphet.

title: A Two-Stage ESM-Based Machine Learning Pipeline for Robust Hierarchically Evaluated Enzyme Function Prediction.
abstract: Accurate enzyme annotation remains a major bottleneck in translating rapidly growing protein sequence data into biological knowledge. Enzyme Commission (EC) prediction is particularly challenging because enzyme functions are organized hierarchically, annotations are often imbalanced across classes, and sequence similarity alone may be insufficient to resolve functional differences. To address these challenges, we developed ESM-ECForest, a 2-stage framework that combines protein embeddings generated by the pretrained language model ESM-2 (Evolutionary Scale Modeling 2) with random forest classifiers. The first stage distinguishes enzymes from nonenzymes, whereas the second assigns one or more EC numbers to proteins predicted to be enzymatic. On an external benchmark comprising 25,778 protein sequences, ESM-ECForest achieved competitive weighted F1 scores among the evaluated off-the-shelf methods, decreasing from 0.94 at Level 1 to 0.90 at Level 4. The largest relative improvements were observed for lyases (EC 4), ligases (EC 6), and translocases (EC 7), although EC 6 and EC 7 remained the most difficult classes internally. Uniform manifold approximation and projection of the ESM-2 embedding space showed clustering patterns that broadly reflected enzyme functional relationships, suggesting that the pretrained representations capture functionally relevant information. These results support the use of pretrained protein language model embeddings as an effective foundation for enzyme annotation. By combining pretrained protein representations with a lightweight supervised classifier, ESM-ECForest provides a scalable approach for EC prediction and may facilitate functional annotation of proteins from large microbial genomic and metagenomic datasets within the taxonomic and EC-label space represented during model development.

title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
abstract: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

title: dictyBase 2026: a reimplementation of the Dictyostelium model organism database on minimal infrastructure.
abstract: Dictyostelium discoideum is a model organism used to investigate a wide array of biological processes including chemotaxis, cell motility, phagocytosis, multicellular development, and autophagy. Many of its genes have human orthologs implicated in disease, making it a useful model organism for studying conditions ranging from cancer to neurodegeneration. dictyBase has served this community for two decades as a home for genomic data, protocols, a stock center, and community news. Here we describe a complete reimplementation of dictyBase as a self-contained service that uses static data files rather than a database server. Each gene record gathers curated function, human-disease context, developmental expression, and protein structure in a single webpage. The site also provides tools for sequence search, genome browsing, enrichment analysis, and experimental design. The complete Dicty Stock Center catalog of 7055 strains and 1265 plasmids is included, and both can be ordered from the site. New literature is curated by an author-in-the-loop pipeline. A language model drafts the annotations, the authors of the paper correct them, and a curator approves them. Analyses can be run on curator-approved annotations alone or extended to include those still awaiting review. dictyBase is freely available at https://dicty.org.

title: Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models generate text by iteratively denoising an entire response in parallel, holding a noisy draft of the answer at every step. We show that these intermediate states surface salient entities early in the denoising trajectory, making them a useful lookahead signal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We further demonstrate that grounding generation in retrieved evidence sharply reduces inter-token dependence, making RAG particularly well suited to parallel decoding. We exploit both through Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models (SARDI), a dynamic RAG framework that uses speculative token predictions to guide retrieval during denoising. SARDI is training-free, retriever-agnostic, and applicable to any reasoning-capable discrete diffusion language model. Across five multi-hop QA benchmarks, SARDI outperforms training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval baselines at up to 4x higher throughput.

title: OmniVIC: A Self-Improving Variable Impedance Controller with Vision-Language In-Context Learning for Safe Robotic Manipulation
abstract: We present OmniVIC, a universal variable impedance controller (VIC) enhanced by a vision language model (VLM), which improves safety and adaptation in any contact-rich robotic manipulation task to enhance safe physical interaction. Traditional VIC have shown advantages when the robot physically interacts with the environment, but lack generalization in unseen, complex, and unstructured safe interactions in universal task scenarios involving contact or uncertainty. To this end, the proposed OmniVIC interprets task context derived reasoning from images and natural language and generates adaptive impedance parameters for a VIC controller. Specifically, the core of OmniVIC is a self-improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation(RAG) and in-context learning (ICL), where RAG retrieves relevant prior experiences from a structured memory bank to inform the controller about similar past tasks, and ICL leverages these retrieved examples and the prompt of current task to query the VLM for generating context-aware and adaptive impedance parameters for the current manipulation scenario. Therefore, a self-improved RAG and ICL guarantee OmniVIC works in universal task scenarios. The impedance parameter regulation is further informed by real-time force/torque feedback to ensure interaction forces remain within safe thresholds. We demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines on a suite of complex contact-rich tasks, both in simulation and on real-world robotic tasks, with improved success rates and reduced force violations. OmniVIC takes a step towards bridging high-level semantic reasoning and low-level compliant control, enabling safer and more generalizable manipulation. Overall, the average success rate increases from 27% (baseline) to 61.4% (OmniVIC).

title: Decompose, Estimate, Select: Coverage-Aware Context Construction for Long-Form RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a language model's output in retrieved evidence, but for complex questions spanning multiple aspects of an information need, relevance-based retrieval may return redundant evidence while leaving some aspects unsupported. We propose a coverage-aware retrieval pipeline that decomposes queries into subquestions, ranks candidates with a coverage-trained bi-encoder, predicts a document\,$\times$\,subquestion coverage matrix with a cross-encoder, and selects documents by greedy maximum-marginal coverage. On TREC RAG 2024, our approach improves $α$-nDCG@10, which rewards newly covered nuggets and discounts redundant evidence, from $0.625$ to $0.702$, approaching the $0.718$ gold-nugget upper bound without sacrificing relevance. We then find that ground-truth oracle retrieval, despite substantially higher retrieval coverage, delivers no more nugget coverage to the answer than our estimated selection. This suggests that answer completeness depends not only on what evidence is retrieved, but also on how effectively the generator uses it. To address this, we introduce a \emph{grounded self-feedback loop} in which the model identifies underused evidence from its first answer and generates again without gold supervision, raising $V_{\mathrm{strict}}$, the fraction of vital reference nuggets fully supported by the answer, by $0.086$ over two passes while largely preserving faithfulness.

title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Complex questions in retrieval-augmented generation require evidence spread over several documents, and an answer is reliable only when the retriever finds all of it. Chain embedding retrievers collect such evidence step by step, re-encoding the question together with the passages retrieved so far, and we find that they are already strong: trained only on gold histories, a small chain embedding retriever that calls no language model outperforms graph-based systems and is competitive with a search agent. This training, however, leaves a gap. At test time the retriever conditions on its own retrievals, which soon contain mistakes: by the third step, about half or more of the states it visits hold a wrong passage, and these passages lower its chance of retrieving a missing gold passage well beyond what the difficulty of the states explains. We propose on-policy state training, which trains the encoder on the states it reaches itself. At every epoch the current encoder retrieves chains for the training questions; each state it visits, including those built on its own mistakes, is labeled with the earliest gold passage still missing while the other missing gold passages are masked, so that no correct continuation is penalized; and the encoder is updated contrastively on these states mixed with teacher-forced ones, so that its training distribution follows it as it learns. The resulting retriever retrieves complete evidence more often than teacher-forced training and the systems we compare, and it transfers without further training to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA that we construct. On the same states, it recovers from its own mistakes far more often, and controlled comparisons attribute the gain to training on the states the encoder currently reaches.

title: Development of an AI-Based smartphone application for rapid tick identification and geospatial mapping: A pilot study.
abstract: Tick-borne diseases, particularly spotted fever group rickettsioses in the western regions of Japan, represent an increasing public health concern. Accurate tick identification is clinically important because pathogen transmission varies by tick genus. However, tick identification is rarely performed in routine clinical practice. Between May 2023 and December 2024, ticks were collected from patients presenting tick bites at 10 medical institutions in Okayama, Hiroshima, and Kagawa prefectures. Additional images of wild ticks were included in the dataset to address class imbalances. Trained personnel morphologically identified all ticks. We developed a two-stage artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline comprising object detection and image classification. Tick regions were detected using a YOLO-based model trained on a publicly available dataset (3258 annotated images), followed by genus-level classification using deep learning models. The system was integrated into a prototype smartphone application with geospatial visualization. The object detection model achieved a mean average precision (mAP@0.5) of 0.954, demonstrating highly accurate tick localization. For classification, a curated dataset of 533 tick images representing four genera was used. The ResNet50 model achieved a mean validation accuracy of 95%, despite substantial class imbalance. Visualization analyses confirmed that the model primarily focused on the morphological features of ticks rather than background elements. We developed the first AI-based smartphone application in Japan for automated tick identification and geospatial visualization. Although limited to genus-level identification and microscope-acquired imaging, this approach may support clinical risk assessment, facilitate patient counseling, reduce unnecessary empirical antibiotic use, and enhance public health surveillance.

title: IBDome: An Integrated Molecular, Histopathological, and Clinical Atlas of Inflammatory Bowel Diseases.
abstract: Multiomic and multimodal datasets with detailed clinical annotations offer significant potential to advance understanding of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), refine diagnostics, and enable personalized therapeutic strategies. In this multicohort study, an extensive multiomic and multimodal analysis of 1002 clinically annotated patients with IBD and non-IBD controls was performed, incorporating whole-exome and RNA sequencing of normal and inflamed gut tissues, serum proteomics, and histopathological assessments from images of H&E-stained tissue sections. Transcriptomic profiles of normal and inflamed tissues revealed distinct site-specific inflammatory signatures in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Leveraging serum proteomics, an inflammatory protein severity signature that reflects underlying intestinal molecular inflammation was developed. Furthermore, foundation model-based deep learning accurately predicted histologic disease activity scores and enabled Crohn's disease vs ulcerative colitis classification from images of H&E-stained intestinal tissue sections, offering a robust tool for clinical evaluation. This integrative, publicly available multiomics resource for IBD research highlights the potential of combining multiomics and advanced computational approaches to improve understanding and management of IBD.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Multiomics Integration in Lung Cancer: From Data Convergence to Precision Phenomics.
abstract: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide due to its extensive molecular heterogeneity, late-stage diagnosis, and therapeutic resistance. Advances in high-throughput omics technologies have enabled comprehensive characterization of tumors across multiple biological layers, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics. However, single-omics analyses provide only fragmented insights into tumor biology, highlighting the need for integrative multiomics approaches. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a powerful tool for integrating heterogeneous datasets and uncovering biologically and clinically relevant patterns. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-driven multiomics integration for lung cancer, highlighting its applications in molecular subtyping, biomarker discovery, prognosis prediction, therapeutic response modeling, and precision oncology. We also discuss current challenges, including data heterogeneity, model interpretability, reproducibility, and clinical translation, together with emerging strategies for integrating multimodal data such as radiomics and digital pathology. Finally, we introduce precision phenomics as a unifying framework that links molecular, spatial, functional, and clinical characteristics of tumors to support personalized cancer management. Collectively, AI-driven multiomics integration has the potential to transform lung cancer research and improve patient outcomes.

analysis_zh:
## 核心内容
该综述聚焦于利用人工智能（机器学习与深度学习）整合肺癌的多组学数据（基因组、表观组、转录组、蛋白质组、代谢组）。其核心在于探讨如何通过AI技术打破单组学分析的局限性，实现从数据汇聚到“精准表型组学”（Precision Phenomics）框架的跨越，以解决肺癌的异质性和耐药性问题。

## 为什么相关
本研究与“foundation_model_agent”主题相关，主要体现在其探讨了AI在处理复杂生物医学大数据中的核心地位。对于蛋白质组学和基因组学研究者而言，该文提供了如何将多维组学数据与临床影像、病理数据整合的系统视角，是理解AI如何辅助临床决策支持系统（CDSS）构建的重要参考。

## 新颖度判断
新颖度较低（1.0）。该文属于综述性质，主要对现有AI在肺癌多组学中的应用进行总结，而非提出新的算法模型或发现新的生物学机制。其贡献在于提出了“精准表型组学”这一统一框架，试图整合空间和功能特征。

## 方法与证据
摘要提到的方法主要为机器学习（ML）和深度学习（DL）。涉及的数据类型涵盖了从分子层面（五大组学）到宏观层面（影像组学、数字病理）的异构数据。证据方面，摘要未列出具体的实验数值或特定数据集（如TCGA或CPTAC）的指标，而是概括了AI在分子分型、预后预测和治疗反应建模中的应用效能。

## 应用价值
该研究的价值在于临床落地指导。通过AI整合多模态数据，可以实现更精确的分子分型和生物标志物鉴定，直接辅助临床医生进行个性化治疗方案的选择。特别是“精准表型组学”框架，为未来开发能够处理空间转录组或空间蛋白质组数据的AI Agent提供了理论基础。

## 局限与风险
摘要明确指出了当前领域的四大挑战：1. **数据异质性**：不同组学平台间的数据难以标准化；2. **模型可解释性**：深度学习的“黑箱”性质限制了临床信任；3. **可重复性**：缺乏统一的基准测试导致模型难以在不同中心间验证；4. **临床转化**：从实验室模型到床旁应用的路径尚不通畅。

title: AI-based multimodal integration of genomics and electronic health records.
abstract: The widespread adoption of electronic health records (EHRs), which capture patient-specific longitudinal information on diagnoses, laboratory tests, clinical procedures, and outcomes, has created unprecedented opportunities to study diseases at scale. Integrating EHR data with genomic information offers novel ways to understand disease heterogeneity, identify biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and predict disease risk to improve clinical decision-making at scale. Recent methodological advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) can handle data with high dimensionality, high levels of noise, and irregular temporality better than traditional statistical approaches. Progress in EHR-linked biobank development, data standardization pipelines, and architectures for modelling and implementation have accelerated the advancement of the field and warrant an assessment of current capabilities and limitations. This Review highlights AI and ML frameworks for integrating genomic, multi-omics, and EHR data, and discusses how these approaches are reshaping genomics research as well as clinical practice.

title: Multi-modal data Integration for Metastatic Risk Prediction of AJCC Stage I/II Melanomas: Results from the Population-based Dutch Early-stage Melanoma Study (D-ESMEL)
abstract: Early-stage melanoma accounts for 40-60% of melanoma-related deaths. Most prognostic modelling studies focus on unimodal approaches or a single multimodal integration strategy, overlooking alternative methods and biological processes underlying metastatic progression. We aimed to evaluate multi-modal data integration for predicting metastasis using the Dutch Early-Stage Melanoma (D-ESMEL) study, the worlds largest multi-modal cohort of American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) stage I/II melanoma. We analysed clinicopathological, genomic, transcriptomic, and pathomics data from the D-ESMEL study. The discovery set included 221 case-control sets matched on follow-up time, age, sex, Breslow thickness, and ulceration. The validation cohort included 154 AJCC stage matched case-control sets based on a population of >5,500 stage I/II melanoma patients. We evaluated four integration strategies (early, intermediate, mixed, and late) using a repeated (n=5) nested 3-fold cross-validation in the discovery set. The best-performing models were evaluated in the validation cohort using the odds ratios (ORs) and a weighted C-index reflecting performance in the sampled population. In the discovery set, intermediate integration of genomics and transcriptomics achieved the highest balanced accuracy ({micro}: 0{middle dot}62; 95% CI: 0{middle dot}57-0{middle dot}66). Early and late integration of transcriptomics and pathomics, and the unimodal transcriptomics model showed similar performance ({micro}: 0{middle dot}61; 95% CI: 0{middle dot}58-0{middle dot}65). In the validation cohort both early integration, late integration, and the unimodal transcriptomics model achieved the highest balanced accuracy of 0{middle dot}60{middle dot} When adjusted for clinicopathological risk factors early integration remained an independent prognostic factor for metastasis (OR 1{middle dot}75; p<0{middle dot}01), outperforming transcriptomics alone (OR 1{middle dot}26; p<0{middle dot}01). Early integration reached a weighted C-index of 0{middle dot}83 outperforming AJCC stage (0{middle dot}81 C-index). When combined the population-weighted C-index was significantly improved to 0{middle dot}85 (p<0{middle dot}01). Early integration of transcriptomics and pathomics outperformed all unimodal models and improved prediction of distant metastasis independently of AJCC stage. Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying these predictions may further support clinical decision-making.

title: Harnessing Extracellular Vesicles for Precision Diagnostics and Infectious Disease Management: Integrating Host- and Pathogen-Derived Cues.
abstract: Conventional infectious disease diagnostics often rely on detecting pathogen-derived factors or an immune response directed against them to diagnose disease. However, these approaches can lack the specificity to distinguish active and latent infections or pathogenic infections from non-pathogenic colonization events. Extracellular vesicles (EVs)-nanoscale vesicles that are abundantly secreted by most cells, particularly in response to disease and cell injury-can carry pathogen-specific factors that indicate the presence and virulence state of a pathogen, as well as immune and inflammatory responses. EVs carrying both types of factors can thus provide valuable information about the presence, identity, and pathogenic phenotype of a microbe in an individual with a suspected infection. Evaluating EVs present in saliva, urine, blood, and other accessible biofluids that contain both host and pathogen information (hpEVs) can thus aid in disease detection, stratification, and monitoring. This review discusses the relevance of EVs to infection and highlights methods that can be used to analyze hpEVs for future clinical applications, including new signal amplification strategies, single vesicle-resolution analysis methods, microfluidic platforms, and AI-based data analysis approaches. It also discusses key challenges that must be addressed to enable development and adoption of hpEV applications for disease diagnosis and management.

title: CryoQSeg: robust particle segmentation for cryo-EM with Qwen-Image-Edit.
abstract: Accurate particle picking remains a critical step in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis, and the field has witnessed the development of a broad spectrum of approaches - from classical template-based methods to modern deep learning frameworks - to address this task. Here we present CryoQSeg, a particle segmentation and picking framework that represents a paradigm shift toward leveraging a state-of-the-art visual large model. Built upon Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 as its core backbone, CryoQSeg is fine-tuned through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on the public CryoPPP benchmark dataset, enabling the generation of high-fidelity, pixel-level particle masks directly from raw micrographs. To translate these masks into precise particle coordinates, we further integrate a hybrid post-processing pipeline that couples Hough circle detection with the segment anything model, forming a seamless end-to-end workflow from raw image input to accurate localization. We evaluate CryoQSeg on five representative benchmark datasets, demonstrating competitive performance across a range of protein types and imaging conditions in comparison to mainstream methods including Topaz and CryoSegNet. Furthermore, we validate the framework on the heterogeneous Crt-SPARTA-gRNA-tDNA complex, where it successfully resolves three distinct oligomeric states - monomer, dimer and tetramer - at high resolutions, despite using a fraction of the micrographs employed in the original study. By bridging modern visual large models with classical and foundation-model-based post-processing strategies, CryoQSeg demonstrates the potential of this emerging paradigm to deliver a robust and automated solution for cryo-EM particle picking, thereby contributing to a solid foundation for high-resolution three-dimensional structural determination of biological macromolecules.

title: Artificial intelligence in pediatric nephrology: current applications and emerging frameworks for evidence generation.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming many areas of medicine. Pediatric nephrology may be a field of particular relevance due to its data-rich environments, rarity of diseases, long-term follow-up needs, and persistent evidence gaps. Traditional clinical research methods, including randomized controlled trials, are often difficult to conduct in pediatric nephrology because of small sample sizes, ethical constraints, heterogeneity of disease, and long latency to clinically meaningful outcomes. AI-based methods offer complementary approaches to address these challenges, spanning diagnostic support, prognostic modeling, imaging analysis, treatment personalization, and innovative frameworks for evidence generation. This narrative review provides a focused overview of AI applications that are already available or emerging in pediatric nephrology, integrating lessons from broader nephrology research on real-world data and digital-twin technologies. We refer to established and near-term applications in chronic kidney disease, dialysis, transplantation, imaging, pathology, and genomics in children. We then discuss future directions, including AI-enabled virtual trials and digital twins as potential tools to extend evidence to pediatric populations traditionally excluded from trials. Ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations specific to children are highlighted. We conclude that AI should be viewed as an adjunct, rather than a replacement to conventional clinical research, with particular promise for advancing precision, inclusivity, and timeliness of evidence in pediatric nephrology.

title: Informed, scalable and unified transport couplings for single-cell alignment and downstream inference with scBIOT
abstract: Single-cell genomics requires methods that account for technical variation while preserving biological signals, remain tractable at atlas scale and support analyses beyond visualization, but existing approaches discard the fitted correspondence that could connect these tasks. Here we introduce scBIOT, a biologically informed optimal-transport framework that formulates single-cell alignment as an explicit and inspectable coupling between cells. scBIOT incorporates prior biological knowledge to preserve known cell identities, compresses transport through prototypes for large datasets and quantifies gene-level changes induced by alignment using coupling-derived transport scores. Across transcriptomic and spatial mapping benchmarks, scBIOT balanced biological conservation, batch correction and label-transfer accuracy while distinguishing batch-associated stress responses from biological immune and drug-response programs. Prototype transport scaled coupling-based analysis to approximately 100 million perturbed cells. Because the coupling encodes probabilistic correspondences rather than only corrected coordinates, the same fitted coupling supports state mapping, trajectory inference, perturbation analysis, multimodal comparison and spatiotemporal localization. Applications to cancer, hematopoiesis and embryonic development identified condition-specific cell states, modality-dependent regulatory programs and spatially resolved developmental transitions. Informed, scalable and unified transport couplings therefore link atlas alignment to downstream biological inference within a single framework.

title: Traumatic brain injury: Multi-omics insights into brain aging, neurodegeneration, and precision therapeutics.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of mortality and persistent neurological disability and is increasingly recognized as a potential contributor to accelerated brain aging and long-term neurodegenerative processes. Beyond the immediate mechanical insult, TBI initiates dynamic secondary injury cascades involving chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic and axonal degeneration, metabolic disturbances, and blood-brain barrier disruption. The persistence and temporal evolution of these molecular alterations may interact with intrinsic aging mechanisms, contributing to progressive neuronal dysfunction and increased vulnerability to age-associated neurodegenerative disorders. The marked biological and temporal heterogeneity of TBI therefore presents major challenges for conventional diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic approaches. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and single-cell and spatial approaches, offer unprecedented opportunities to characterize the molecular trajectories linking TBI, brain aging, and neurodegeneration. Integrative multi-omics frameworks, coupled with network biology, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and causal inference, enable the identification of molecular signatures, age-related regulatory networks, clinically relevant biomarkers, and therapeutically actionable targets. This review synthesizes emerging multi-omics insights into the molecular mechanisms through which TBI may influence brain aging and neurodegenerative progression, with particular emphasis on phase-specific molecular signatures, biomarker discovery, patient stratification, therapeutic target prioritization, and precision neurotherapeutics. We further discuss longitudinal profiling, single-cell and spatial approaches, and AI-assisted modeling for patient stratification and therapeutic optimization. Integrating multi-omics with systems biology may provide a framework for studying TBI-associated brain aging and developing personalized interventions, although prospective clinical validation remains essential.

title: Artificial intelligence for predicting BCG response in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer: a systematic review.
abstract: To systematically identify, appraise and synthesise artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) models that predict treatment response and clinical outcomes after intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), a setting in which current risk calculators underperform, and identifying non-responders has become urgent as alternatives to BCG enter practice. PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science were searched through April 2026 following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews [PROSPERO] number CRD420261376808). Studies developing or validating AI/ML models for BCG-associated outcomes with a quantitative performance metric were included. Risk of bias was assessed with the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST). Evidence was synthesised along a clinically oriented framework: AI as a perceptual tool (extracting signal from histology or imaging) or integrative tool (re-weighting clinicopathological, molecular, or urinary variables). A total of 15 studies (>24 900 patients) were included: seven perceptual, eight integrative. By input data, six used digital pathology, two radiomics, two genomics/transcriptomics, four clinicopathological markers, and one urinary biomarkers. The digital-pathology Computational Histology Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) platform, validated across 12 international centres, stratified high-grade recurrence (hazard ratio [HR] 2.08), progression (HR 3.87) and BCG-unresponsive disease (HR 2.31), and was the only model providing a first signal of predictive value, demonstrating a significant BCG vs gemcitabine/docetaxel interaction (P = 0.029). Integrative models PROGRxN-BCa (concordance index [C-index] 0.79) and DeepSurv (C-index 0.881) outperformed standard calculators but with modest gains (ΔC-index 0.05-0.10). Only 40% of studies performed external validation, none prospectively; five were at high risk of bias. Perceptual AI, particularly digital pathology, has the highest external validation and provides the only biomarker with a first signal of predictive value for BCG vs alternatives, increasingly relevant in the context of the global BCG shortage. Integrative models such as PROGRxN-BCa and DeepSurv outperform standard calculators with incremental gains and are freely accessible. Prospective validation, systematic calibration reporting and treatment-by-biomarker interaction analyses, ideally embedded in trials such as the BRIDGE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05538663), remain priorities before clinical adoption.

title: AI-Driven Multiomics Biomarkers for Precision Oncology: Navigating the Translational Gap and Regulatory Hurdles.
abstract: The discussion on precision oncology integrates multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence, specifically addressing biomarker discovery and personalized therapeutic strategies. In this way, clinical translation and multiomics biomarkers are reconstructed challenges such as heterogeneity, validate, algorithmic bias, regulatory complexities, and ethical issues. This review critically evaluates how advanced technologies operating in an integrated manner facilitate precision oncology by supporting fields such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and radiomics. To conduct the study, we performed literature search using standard databases such as PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, focusing on papers published between 2020 and 2025. We address the all aspects of biomarker identification and clinical applications; we employed a five-stage framework comprising multiparametric data generation, integration, biomarker discovery, rigorous validation, and regulatory implementation. To further examine this review, we have employed emerging computational approaches, including machine learning and deep learning and graph neural networks alongside regulatory frameworks and ethical, legal, and social considerations. Discussing translation barriers, we consider factors such as limited reproducibility, validation, and critical discussion particularly studies. Ultimately, a future model based on standardized, validated, and transparent learning strategies accelerates and fosters the development of clinically reliable standards. Our review provides an integrative roadmap for modern, multiomics-driven biomarker approaches in precision oncology practice.

title: Origin Lens: A Privacy-First Mobile Framework for Cryptographic Image Provenance and AI Detection
abstract: The proliferation of generative AI poses challenges for information integrity assurance, requiring systems that connect model governance with end-user verification. We present Origin Lens, a privacy-first mobile framework that targets visual disinformation through a layered verification architecture. Unlike server-side detection systems, Origin Lens performs cryptographic image provenance verification and metadata-based AI detection locally on the device via a Rust/Flutter hybrid architecture. Our system integrates multiple signals - including cryptographic provenance, generative-model metadata and watermarks, and optional retrieval-augmented verification - to provide users with graded confidence indicators at the point of consumption. We discuss the framework's alignment with regulatory requirements (EU AI Act, DSA) and its role in verification infrastructure that complements platform-level mechanisms.

title: Adaptive Modular Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Cross-Domain Image Classification
abstract: Effective image classification in real-world scenarios requires models capable of capturing both local features and global context, while adapting to the evolving complexity of the input. This paper presents a hybrid deep learning system named AMR-Net (Adaptive Modular Retrieval Network) for adaptable image classification in environmental and industrial contexts. The proposed model integrates ResNet-based local feature extraction and Vision Transformer-based global representation learning with an FAISS-based memory retrieval module for contextual enhancement. Furthermore, AMR-Net has an adaptive modular extension mechanism to dynamically enhance network capacity when validation performance plateaus during training. The proposed framework was evaluated using a ten-class waste classification dataset and the Kolektor Surface Defect Dataset 2 (KolektorSDD2), achieving classification accuracies of 97.15% and 99.80%, respectively. Experimental results demonstrate that AMR-Net consistently outperforms mainstream convolutional and transformer-based approaches while maintaining robust cross-domain generalization. Component-wise ablation studies show that global attention (ViT), retrieval-based contextual learning (FAISS), and adaptive modular growth each provide complementary and partially overlapping contributions to overall performance, with global attention contributing the largest individual gain. The proposed architecture is a scalable and flexible solution for image classification challenges characterized by data unpredictability, class imbalance, and dynamic feature distributions.

title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.
